topics.title: Views and view controllers
topics.summary: The two pieces everything else is built from: the rectangle that draws something on screen, and the object that owns a whole screenful of them.

lesson.heading: Everything you can see is a UIView
lesson.body:
In UIKit, every single thing on screen is a **`UIView`**. Not "most things" — every one. A `UIView` is a rectangle that knows where it is, how big it is, and how to draw itself.

A button, a label, an image, a switch: they are all `UIView` with extra behaviour added on top. `UILabel` is a `UIView` that knows how to draw text. `UIButton` is a `UIView` that knows how to react to a tap. When you learn what a `UIView` can do, you have learned something that applies to all of them.

Underneath, a `UIView` does not actually draw anything itself. It owns a **`CALayer`**, and the layer does the drawing — that is why rounded corners, shadows and borders are all set on `view.layer` rather than on the view. The view adds the things a layer does not know about: handling touches and taking part in layout.

That split is worth remembering, because it explains an everyday oddity: `view.layer.cornerRadius` rounds the corners, but a layer knows nothing about taps, so you still handle those on the view.
lesson.code:
let box = UIView()
box.backgroundColor = .systemBlue
box.layer.cornerRadius = 12       // drawing goes through the layer
box.layer.borderWidth = 1

let label = UILabel()             // a label is a UIView too
label.text = "Hello"
label.textColor = .label          // adapts to light and dark

let button = UIButton(type: .system)   // and so is a button
button.setTitle("Confirm", for: .normal)

lesson.heading: Views inside views: the hierarchy
lesson.body:
Views are arranged in a **tree**. A view can contain other views, which can contain others in turn. The contained ones are called **subviews**, and the one containing them is the **superview**.

The tree does three things at once. It decides **what draws on top of what**: subviews are drawn in the order they were added, so the last one added appears in front. It decides **where things are**: a subview's position is measured from its superview's top-left corner. And it decides **who stays alive**: a superview holds its subviews, so when it goes, they go too.

There is one asymmetry people trip over: you add a child to a parent, but you remove the child from itself. `parent.addSubview(child)` to put it in, `child.removeFromSuperview()` to take it out. There is no `removeSubview`.

If you need to change the order afterwards, `bringSubviewToFront` and `sendSubviewToBack` move a view within its siblings without removing it.
lesson.code:
container.addSubview(a)
container.addSubview(b)   // b is drawn ON TOP of a: it was added later

container.subviews        // [a, b] — in drawing order
b.superview               // container

container.bringSubviewToFront(a)   // now a is the one in front
a.removeFromSuperview()            // called on the child, not the parent

lesson.heading: frame, bounds and center
lesson.body:
These three describe where a view is, and the difference between the first two is asked at almost every interview.

**`frame`** is the view **seen from outside**: its position and size measured in its superview's coordinates. "This box starts 40 points from the left of its parent."

**`bounds`** is the view **seen from inside**: its own coordinate system. Its origin is normally `(0, 0)` — "as far as I am concerned, I start here" — and its size is the same as the frame's.

**`center`** is the middle of the frame, in the superview's coordinates. Changing it moves the view; it is often handier than recalculating the whole frame.

Two cases make the distinction real rather than theoretical:

**A rotated view.** Apply a `transform` and `bounds` does not move: inside, the view is still the same rectangle it always was. But `frame` grows to become the smallest upright box that encloses the rotated view. (This is also why you must never set `frame` on a view with a transform.)

**A scroll view.** Scrolling does not move the content. It moves the scroll view's own `bounds.origin` — which is exactly what `contentOffset` is. The content sits perfectly still; the window you look through it slides.
lesson.code:
let v = UIView(frame: CGRect(x: 40, y: 60, width: 100, height: 50))
v.frame     // (40, 60, 100, 50)  where I am, for my parent
v.bounds    // ( 0,  0, 100, 50)  where I am, for myself
v.center    // (90, 85)           the middle, for my parent

v.transform = CGAffineTransform(rotationAngle: .pi / 4)   // 45 degrees
v.bounds    // unchanged: inside, nothing happened
v.frame     // bigger: the upright box that now encloses it

// Scrolling 100 points down
scrollView.contentOffset.y   // 100
scrollView.bounds.origin.y   // 100 — the same number, the same thing

lesson.heading: The view controller: who owns a screen
lesson.body:
A view is a rectangle. A **`UIViewController`** is the object that owns a whole screenful of them and takes care of its life: building it, filling it with data, reacting to what the user does, tidying up afterwards.

Every controller has a `view` property, and that view is the root of everything on that screen. Everything else hangs off it.

That view is created **lazily**: not when the controller is created, but the first time somebody actually reads `view`. This matters more than it sounds. In `init` the view does not exist yet, so anything from a storyboard is still `nil`. Touching the interface there either crashes or, worse, quietly creates the view too early.

The right place for setup is **`viewDidLoad`**, which runs once, just after the view exists. And the first line should always be `super.viewDidLoad()`, because the parent class has its own work to do there.

lesson.heading: Code, XIB or Storyboard
lesson.body:
There are three ways to build an interface in UIKit, and teams argue about them. It is worth knowing what each actually is.

**In code.** You create the views and lay them out by writing it. More lines, but everything is explicit, it is easy to read in a code review, and two people editing the same screen do not fight over the file.

**XIB (or nib).** One file describing one view, edited visually. Quick to see, and small enough that reviewing it stays manageable.

**Storyboard.** Many screens plus the arrows between them, in one file. Lovely at the start of a project and painful later: the file is XML, and two people editing it at once produces a merge conflict nobody enjoys.

From a XIB or storyboard, two connections link the design to your code. An **`@IBOutlet`** is a property pointing at a view in the file. An **`@IBAction`** is a method the file calls when something happens — a tap, a value changing.

Outlets are declared `UILabel!` with an exclamation mark for a reason: they really are empty until the view loads, and only then does the system fill them in. That is why they are `nil` in `init` and safe in `viewDidLoad`.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a kind of `UIView`?
questions.explanation: A view controller is not something you can see: it is the object that **owns** a screenful of views and looks after their life. It has a `view` property, but it is not one itself. Everything else in the list is a rectangle that draws something.
whyWrong: A label is a `UIView` that knows how to draw text.
A stack view is a `UIView` that lines up its children for you.
An image view is a `UIView` that knows how to draw a picture.

questions.prompt: After this code, which view is in front?
options: b, because it was added last
a, because it was added first
It depends on zPosition, which is equal here
questions.explanation: Subviews are drawn in the order they were added, so each new one lands on top of what is already there. `b` came last, so `b` is in front. To change it afterwards without removing anything, use `bringSubviewToFront`.
whyWrong: First added means first drawn, so it is furthest back, not in front.
`zPosition` can override the order, but when it is the same for both, it is the order in `subviews` that decides.
There is no halfway: one of the two is drawn over the other.

questions.prompt: What is `v.bounds.origin` here?
questions.code: let v = UIView(frame: CGRect(x: 40, y: 60, width: 100, height: 50))
questions.explanation: `bounds` is the view seen from inside, in its own coordinates, where it always starts at `(0, 0)` — "as far as I am concerned, I begin here". The 40 and 60 are where it sits for its parent, and that is `frame`.
whyWrong: (40, 60) is `frame.origin`: the position seen from the parent, not from inside.
(90, 85) is `center`, the middle of the frame measured in the parent's coordinates.
(100, 50) is the size, not an origin. It appears in both `frame.size` and `bounds.size`.

questions.prompt: How do you take a view out of the hierarchy?
options: Call `removeFromSuperview()` on the view you want out
questions.explanation: The asymmetry is deliberate: you add a child to a parent, but you remove the child from itself. `removeFromSuperview()` takes it out of the tree and, unless somebody else is holding it, frees it.
whyWrong: There is no such method. Adding goes through the parent, removing goes through the child.
`superview` is read-only: you can look at it, you cannot assign to it.
`frame` is a `CGRect` and can never be `nil`. Changing it moves the view, it does not remove it.

questions.prompt: Where does the interface a `UIViewController` manages actually live?
options: In its `view` property, which is the root of all the rest
Straight in the `UIWindow`, with nothing in between
questions.explanation: Every controller has one root `view`, and everything on that screen hangs off it. That is also what gets added to the window or to a parent controller's view when the screen is shown.
whyWrong: The window holds the root controller's view, not every view one by one.
A controller has no `subviews`. Only views do.
A controller has no `layer` either. Layers belong to views.

questions.prompt: You rotate a view 45 degrees with a transform. What happens to `frame` and `bounds`?
questions.code: v.transform = CGAffineTransform(rotationAngle: .pi / 4)
options: `bounds` stays the same, `frame` becomes the upright box that encloses it
Both change in the same way
Neither changes: a transform only affects drawing
questions.explanation: Inside, the view has not changed: it is the same rectangle, so `bounds` is untouched. Seen from outside it is now tilted, and `frame` has to be a plain upright rectangle, so it becomes the smallest one that encloses the rotated view — which is bigger. This is also why you must not set `frame` on a transformed view.
whyWrong: They cannot change the same way: one is measured inside, the other outside, and only the outside view is tilted.
It is exactly the other way round: `bounds` is the one that stays put.
The transform really does change the geometry seen from outside — `frame` is different afterwards.

questions.prompt: When is a `UIViewController`'s `view` created?
options: The first time somebody reads the `view` property
Only if it came from a storyboard
questions.explanation: It is lazy: the controller can exist for a long time with no view at all, which saves memory for screens you prepared but never showed. The view is built on first access, and immediately afterwards `viewDidLoad` runs.
whyWrong: In `init` the view does not exist yet. That is exactly why outlets are `nil` there.
Being freed is the end of its life, not the start.
The source makes no difference: from code, XIB or storyboard, it is always lazy.

questions.prompt: Why is an `@IBOutlet` `nil` inside the view controller's `init`?
options: Because outlets are connected when the view loads, which happens after init
Because outlets are always weak and die immediately
Because `private` stops the file writing to them
Because the label has not been added to a superview yet
questions.explanation: The system fills in the outlets while it loads the view from the file, and that happens after `init`. That is why they are declared with `!` — they really are empty for a while — and why `viewDidLoad` is the first safe place to use them.
whyWrong: `weak` is not the reason. Even a strong outlet is `nil` before the view has loaded.
`private` only limits who can see it in your code; the loading machinery still reaches it.
It has not been created yet at all, let alone added anywhere.

questions.prompt: In a `UIScrollView`, what changes when you scroll the content down by 100 points?
options: `bounds.origin.y` goes up by 100: that is what `contentOffset` is
Nothing in the scroll view's own geometry: only the subviews move
questions.explanation: The content never moves. What moves is the scroll view's own window onto it: `bounds.origin` slides, and the subviews — which are positioned relative to those bounds — appear to shift. `contentOffset` is not a separate thing: it is literally `bounds.origin`.
whyWrong: `frame` is where the scroll view sits in its parent, and that does not change while you scroll inside it.
`center` is derived from `frame`, which is not moving either.
The subviews do not move at all: their positions stay exactly where they were. The viewport is what shifts.

questions.prompt: What actually draws a `UIView`'s content on screen?
options: Its `CALayer`: the view adds touches and layout on top
The view itself; the layer is only for animations
The `UIWindow`, which draws for every view in the tree
questions.explanation: Every view owns a layer, and the layer does the drawing. The view wraps it with the things a layer knows nothing about: receiving touches, taking part in Auto Layout, responding to the responder chain. That is why corner radius, shadows and borders are all set on `view.layer`.
whyWrong: Layers are not only for animations: they are what gets drawn, animated or not.
The window is itself just a view at the top of the tree. It does not draw for anyone else.
A controller coordinates. It never draws anything.

topics.title: The life of a screen
topics.summary: Which method runs when, what you can safely do in each, and why reading a view's size too early gives you the wrong number.

lesson.heading: The order things happen in
lesson.body:
A view controller does not just appear. It goes through a sequence of steps, and each one has a method you can override. Putting your code in the wrong one is the single most common beginner bug in UIKit.

The order, the first time a screen is shown:

**`loadView`** — the view is created. You almost never touch this.
**`viewDidLoad`** — the view now exists. **Runs once.** This is where you build subviews, set colours, register cells.
**`viewWillAppear`** — about to come on screen. **Runs every time**, including coming back from another screen.
**`viewIsAppearing`** — on its way in, and by now the size is correct. Also every time.
**`viewDidLayoutSubviews`** — the layout has just been worked out. Can run **many times**.
**`viewDidAppear`** — fully on screen, the animation is over.

And on the way out, `viewWillDisappear` then `viewDidDisappear`.

The rule that follows: **things you do once go in `viewDidLoad`; things that must be fresh each time go in `viewWillAppear`.** Refreshing data in `viewDidLoad` means it is stale when the user comes back from another screen.

lesson.heading: Sizes are not ready in viewDidLoad
lesson.body:
This catches everybody. In `viewDidLoad` the view exists, but **nobody has worked out how big it is yet**. You usually get the size from the storyboard or a placeholder, not the real one on this device.

So code like `view.bounds.width / 2` gives a plausible but wrong number, and it works on the simulator you tested and breaks on a different screen size.

The layout happens afterwards, and two methods run once it has:

**`viewIsAppearing`** — the newer one. It runs before the screen is visible and the geometry is already correct, so it is the right place for anything that needs the real size before the user sees it. It only runs when the screen appears.

**`viewDidLayoutSubviews`** — runs every time the layout is recalculated: rotation, keyboard, a change in content. Use it for things that must track the size, but keep it cheap and never start an animation from it, because it can run many times in a row.

In practice: if you are writing constraints with Auto Layout, you rarely need either of these. The need for them comes up when you are setting frames by hand.

lesson.heading: loadView, and putting one controller inside another
lesson.body:
**`loadView`** is where the root view is created. You override it in only one case: when you want the root view to be a class of your own instead of a plain `UIView`.

When you do, there is one rule: assign `view` and **do not call `super.loadView()`**. The parent's version builds a plain view, and calling it would just make one for nothing.

The other thing in this lesson is **containment**: putting a controller inside another, so that a screen is made of pieces each with its own logic. A tab bar and a navigation controller are both doing this.

There are four steps and people forget the last one:

`addChild(child)` — tell the parent.
`view.addSubview(child.view)` — put the view in.
position it.
`child.didMove(toParent: self)` — tell the child it is done.

Miss `didMove` and the child does not get its appearance callbacks properly, so `viewWillAppear` fires at the wrong moment or not at all. On the way out the order is reversed, and there `willMove(toParent: nil)` is the one that gets forgotten.

lesson.heading: Presenting a screen over another
lesson.body:
There are two ways to get to a new screen, and they behave differently.

**Push**, inside a navigation controller: the new screen replaces the old one. The old one gets `viewWillDisappear` and `viewDidDisappear`, because it really is no longer visible.

**Present**, modally: the new screen comes up over the old one. Since iOS 13 the default style is a card that does not cover the whole screen, and the one underneath stays visible — so it gets **neither** `viewWillDisappear` nor `viewDidDisappear`.

This trips people up constantly: you put a refresh in `viewWillAppear`, the user closes the card, and nothing refreshes, because as far as UIKit is concerned that screen never went away.

If you need to know when the card is dismissed, do not rely on appearance callbacks. Pass a closure back, use a delegate, or implement `UIAdaptivePresentationControllerDelegate` to catch the swipe-down too — because the user can also dismiss a card by dragging it, without touching any button of yours.

lesson.heading: The life of the whole app
lesson.body:
Above individual screens there is the life of the app itself. Since iOS 13 it is split in two: the **`AppDelegate`** handles things that concern the whole process, and the **`SceneDelegate`** handles each window — because on iPad an app can have several.

If you build the window in code, that goes in `scene(_:willConnectTo:options:)`, not in the app delegate. Doing it in the app delegate is the most common mistake when moving older code over.

The states you need to know, and what belongs in each:

**Active** — in the foreground and receiving taps.
**Inactive** — visible, but not receiving: a phone call, the control centre, the app switcher. Pause a game here.
**Background** — not visible. You have a few seconds. Save what must not be lost.
**Suspended** — frozen in memory. No code runs, and the system may kill you without warning.

When the user presses Home: first `sceneWillResignActive` (I am stepping away), then `sceneDidEnterBackground` (I am gone). Coming back, the reverse. Saving in `willResignActive` is too early and in `didEnterBackground` is right — that is the last callback you are guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Which of these runs **only once** per load of the view?
questions.explanation: `viewDidLoad` runs just after the view has been created, and the view is only created once. That is why it is the place for setup that must not be repeated: building subviews, registering cells, setting colours.
whyWrong: `viewWillAppear` runs every time the screen comes on, including when you come back to it from another one.
`viewDidLayoutSubviews` can run many times, even several in a row, whenever the layout is recalculated.
`viewDidAppear` runs every time, just like `viewWillAppear`, only a bit later.

questions.prompt: In what order are these printed the first time the screen is shown?
questions.explanation: The order follows the steps: the view is created (A), it exists (B), it is about to appear (C), the layout is worked out (D), it is fully on screen (E). The layout always happens before the screen is actually visible, because something has to be drawn.
whyWrong: `viewDidLoad` cannot come before `loadView`: there would be no view to have loaded.
The layout comes after `viewWillAppear`, not before: UIKit announces the appearance first and then measures.
`viewDidAppear` is last. Being on screen means the layout is already finished.

questions.prompt: Why can reading `view.bounds.width` in `viewDidLoad` give you the wrong number?
options: The view does not exist yet
Nothing has been laid out yet: the size is not final
questions.explanation: The view exists, but nobody has measured it for this device yet. You get whatever it came with — the size from the storyboard, or a placeholder. The real size is ready in `viewIsAppearing` and in `viewDidLayoutSubviews`.
whyWrong: It is not zero: it holds a plausible value, which is worse, because the bug looks like it works.
`viewDidLoad` always runs on the main thread, like everything else in UIKit.
It does exist: `viewDidLoad` runs precisely because it has just been created.

questions.prompt: What happens here, with `titleLabel` an `@IBOutlet` from a storyboard?
questions.code:
let vc = storyboard.instantiateViewController(
    identifier: "Detail") as! DetailViewController
vc.titleLabel.text = "Hello"
present(vc, animated: true)
options: It works: instantiating connects the outlets
It crashes: the outlet is still nil because the view is not loaded
The text is applied later, in viewDidAppear
questions.explanation: Creating the controller does not create its view, and the outlets are only connected when the view loads. So `titleLabel` is `nil` and the `!` in its declaration turns that into a crash. The fix is to pass the text as a property and apply it in `viewDidLoad`.
whyWrong: Instantiating only creates the controller. The view, and with it the outlets, come later.
Nothing is ignored: it is a crash, loud and immediate.
Nothing gets remembered for later. The line runs now, on a `nil`.

questions.prompt: A presents B modally with the default style. What does A receive?
options: Both, exactly as with a push
questions.explanation: Since iOS 13 the default is a card that does not cover the whole screen, so A is still visible and UIKit considers it still on screen. Neither disappear callback fires. That is why a refresh placed in `viewWillAppear` does not run when the card is closed.
whyWrong: Neither fires, not just one of them, because A never actually leaves the screen.
A push is different: there the old screen really does go away and does get both.
The animation changes nothing. What matters is whether A stays visible.

questions.prompt: In a scene-based app, where do you create the `UIWindow` in code?
questions.explanation: Since iOS 13 each window belongs to a scene, and the scene tells you it is ready in `willConnectTo`. The app delegate deals with the whole process, not with individual windows — which matters on iPad, where one app can have several.
whyWrong: That is where it went before iOS 13. With scenes, the app delegate no longer owns the window.
A controller lives inside the window: it cannot create the thing that contains it.
`didBecomeActive` happens later, and runs again every time you come back. The window would be built more than once.

questions.prompt: What is missing from this containment code?
questions.code:
let child = MapViewController()
addChild(child)
view.addSubview(child.view)
child.view.frame = view.bounds
questions.explanation: Adding a child has four steps and this is the last one: telling the child the move is finished. Without it the appearance callbacks do not line up, so the child's `viewWillAppear` fires at the wrong moment or not at all.
whyWrong: `willMove(toParent:)` is called for you by `addChild`. The one you have to call yourself is `didMove`, at the end.
`loadView` is never called by hand: the view is built on its own when it is first needed.
It is not complete: without `didMove` the child does not know it has arrived.

questions.prompt: When does `viewIsAppearing(_:)` run?
options: Between `viewWillAppear` and `viewDidAppear`, with the geometry already correct
Only when the trait collection changes
questions.explanation: It was added to fill a gap: a point where the screen is not visible yet but the sizes are already right. Before it, you had to choose between `viewWillAppear` (too early, wrong sizes) and `viewDidLayoutSubviews` (right sizes, but runs many times).
whyWrong: It comes after `viewWillAppear`, not before, and it runs every time the screen appears.
It happens before `viewDidAppear`, which is exactly what makes it useful: you can still fix things invisibly.
Trait changes have their own callback. This one is about appearing.

questions.prompt: The user presses Home while the app is active. In what order do the callbacks arrive?
questions.explanation: First the app stops receiving taps but is still visible (`willResignActive` — pause a game here), then it actually leaves the screen (`didEnterBackground`). The second is the last callback you are guaranteed, so that is where you save.
whyWrong: The order is reversed: you cannot be in the background before you have stopped being active.
In a scene-based app the scene callbacks are the ones that arrive. The app delegate ones are for the whole process.
`didDisconnect` is when the window is thrown away entirely, which is a different and much rarer event.

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to override `loadView` to use your own root view?
options: Call `super.loadView()` and then add your view as a subview
Assign `view` in `init` and leave the override empty
questions.explanation: `loadView` has one job: decide what the root view is. Assign it and stop. Calling `super` would build a plain `UIView` that is thrown away a moment later — wasteful, and a sign of not understanding what the method is for.
whyWrong: That gives you two views instead of one: the plain one from `super` with yours inside it.
`loadView` is never called by hand. The system calls it when the view is first needed.
In `init` it is too early, and assigning `view` there forces the view to load immediately, defeating the laziness.

topics.title: Auto Layout: describing where things go
topics.summary: Instead of giving coordinates, you state rules — and the system works out the numbers for every screen size. The rules, the priorities, and the three words that decide who shrinks.

lesson.heading: A constraint is a sentence about two views
lesson.body:
Before Auto Layout you gave each view a position and a size in numbers. That works on one screen size and breaks on the next.

Auto Layout turns it round. You do not say "this label starts at 16 points"; you say **"this label's left edge is 16 points from its parent's left edge"**. The system collects all those sentences and works out the actual numbers for whatever screen the app is running on.

Each sentence is a **constraint**, and it always has the same shape: *one view's edge = another view's edge, plus or minus something, maybe times something*.

The edges have names — `leadingAnchor`, `trailingAnchor`, `topAnchor`, `bottomAnchor`, `widthAnchor`, `centerXAnchor` — and you join two of them with `constraint(equalTo:)`.

**Leading and trailing, not left and right.** Leading is where reading starts: the left in English and Italian, the right in Arabic. Using leading means your interface mirrors itself correctly in those languages, free of charge.

And the one line everybody forgets: **`translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false`** on any view you created in code. Without it, UIKit quietly adds its own constraints from the view's frame, those fight with yours, and the console fills up with complaints.

lesson.heading: Priorities: what to give up when it does not fit
lesson.body:
Sometimes the rules cannot all be satisfied at once. "Be 300 wide" and "never wider than the parent minus 40" cannot both hold on a 320-point screen.

So each constraint has a **priority**, a number from 1 to 1000. 1000 means **required**: it must hold, no argument. Anything below is a preference: the system satisfies it if it can, and gives it up if it must, starting with the lowest.

The named values you will actually use: `.required` is 1000, `.defaultHigh` is 750, `.defaultLow` is 250.

There is one rule that surprises people and is worth remembering: **once a constraint is active, you cannot change a required priority to anything else, or anything else to required**. Doing it raises an exception while the app runs. If you need a priority to change, start it just below required — 999 — and move it from there.

When two required constraints genuinely conflict, Auto Layout does not crash. It breaks one of them, shows something, and prints a long complaint in the console. That log is the thing to read: it names the constraints and tells you which one it dropped.

lesson.heading: Who stretches and who shrinks
lesson.body:
Some views know how big they want to be. A label knows how much room its text needs; a button knows its title plus its padding. That natural size is the **`intrinsicContentSize`**, and it means you often do not need width and height constraints at all.

When two such views share a row, two questions come up, and each has a word of its own.

**There is space left over — who stretches?** That is **content hugging**: how much a view wants to stay wrapped around its content. The one with **lower** hugging gives in and stretches. Remember it as "the one that hugs itself less tightly is the one that lets go".

**There is not enough space — who shrinks?** That is **compression resistance**: how much a view refuses to be squeezed. The one with **lower** resistance is the one that gets truncated.

So: *higher hugging = does not stretch. Higher resistance = does not shrink.*

And a detail worth knowing. If a custom view works out its own intrinsic size, changing what it contains does not update the layout by itself: you have to say so, with `invalidateIntrinsicContentSize()`.

lesson.heading: UIStackView: constraints you do not have to write
lesson.body:
Most layouts are a row or a column of things. Writing the constraints for that by hand is five lines per view, and it has to be redone whenever you insert something in the middle.

**`UIStackView`** does it for you. You give it the views in order, say whether it is a row or a column, and it produces the constraints itself. The properties that matter:

**`axis`** — horizontal or vertical.
**`spacing`** — the gap between items.
**`distribution`** — how the space along the axis is shared: `.fill` (the default, somebody stretches), `.fillEqually` (everyone the same), `.equalSpacing` (natural sizes, equal gaps).
**`alignment`** — how they line up across the axis: `.fill`, `.center`, `.leading`.

The feature that makes it genuinely worth it: setting `isHidden = true` on a view inside a stack **takes it out of the layout entirely**, and the others close the gap, animatably. Everywhere else in UIKit, a hidden view still occupies its space. This one behaviour removes an enormous amount of constraint juggling.

One thing to watch: you add views with `addArrangedSubview`, not `addSubview`. The second one puts the view in without the stack managing it, and then nothing lines up and nothing is obviously wrong.

lesson.heading: When the layout actually happens
lesson.body:
Changing a constraint does not move anything straight away. UIKit notes that something needs redoing and works it out at the end of the current cycle, all at once. That is deliberate: twenty changes cost one layout pass instead of twenty.

The three methods, and what each one really means:

**`setNeedsLayout()`** — "something has changed, redo it at the next opportunity". Cheap, returns immediately.
**`layoutIfNeeded()`** — "redo it **now**, before this line finishes". Costly, but sometimes necessary.
**`layoutSubviews()`** — this is the method UIKit calls. You override it, you never call it.

This explains the classic failure: putting `constraint.constant = 200` inside an animation block does nothing. The animation block records what changes **during it**, and nothing changed yet — the layout happens later, outside it, so the view jumps.

The fix is to change the constant first, and then call `layoutIfNeeded()` **inside** the block. That forces the recalculation to happen within the animation, and now there is something to animate.

questions.prompt: Two labels in a row, and there is space left over. Which one stretches?
questions.code:
left.setContentHuggingPriority(.init(251), for: .horizontal)
right.setContentHuggingPriority(.init(250), for: .horizontal)
options: Neither: the layout is ambiguous and it crashes
questions.explanation: Hugging is how much a view wants to stay wrapped around its content. The one that wants it less — the lower number — is the one that gives in and stretches. Here `right` is 250 against 251, so `right` stretches.
whyWrong: Higher hugging means the opposite: it holds on to its natural size and does not stretch.
They cannot both stretch: the two priorities are different, and that difference is exactly what decides.
There is nothing ambiguous here, and anyway Auto Layout does not crash on a conflict: it breaks a constraint and logs it.

questions.prompt: You add constraints to a view made in code and the console complains about `NSAutoresizingMaskLayoutConstraint`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The view has no intrinsic size
questions.explanation: By default UIKit turns a view's frame into its own set of constraints, so that old code keeps working. Those collide with the ones you wrote. The line switches that off and is the first thing to check whenever you see that name in the log.
whyWrong: They do exactly the same thing. `activate` is just the tidier way to turn several on at once.
Not having an intrinsic size would mean missing constraints, not a conflict with autoresizing ones.
Required priorities can conflict, but the name in the message points straight at the autoresizing mask.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
options: It crashes: constraints cannot change inside an animation
Nothing animates: the view jumps on the next layout pass
questions.explanation: The animation block records changes that happen while it runs. Changing a constant only marks the layout as needing redoing — the recalculation happens afterwards, outside the block, so there is nothing to animate and the view jumps. Change the constant first, then call `layoutIfNeeded()` inside the block.
whyWrong: That is what it looks like it should do, which is why the mistake is so common.
Nothing crashes: changing a constant is perfectly legal anywhere.
The timing has nothing to do with it. Even long after `viewDidAppear`, it still jumps.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `setNeedsLayout()` and `layoutIfNeeded()`?
options: The first is immediate, the second waits for the next cycle
The first marks it for later, the second does it right now
The first updates constraints, the second redraws
questions.explanation: `setNeedsLayout` leaves a note: "redo this at the next opportunity". It is cheap and returns at once. `layoutIfNeeded` does it immediately, before the next line runs — which is why it is the one you put inside an animation block.
whyWrong: They are opposites in timing, which is the whole reason both exist.
It is the other way round: `setNeedsLayout` is the one that waits.
Neither one redraws. Redrawing is `setNeedsDisplay`, a different matter entirely.

questions.prompt: Two labels do not fit in the row. Which one gets truncated?
questions.code:
name.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(.init(750), for: .horizontal)
price.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(.init(751), for: .horizontal)
options: Neither: it runs off the screen
questions.explanation: Compression resistance is how much a view refuses to be squeezed. The one that refuses less — the lower number — is the one that gives. `name` is 750 against 751, so `name` gets the ellipsis. This is the standard setup for a row with a label and a price: the price must stay readable.
whyWrong: Higher resistance means it holds its full size: that is the one that stays whole.
The two priorities are different, so Auto Layout picks one. Proportional shrinking would need equal values.
Nothing runs off: Auto Layout always produces something that fits, by squeezing whoever resists least.

questions.prompt: What happens when this line runs on an active constraint created as required?
questions.code: widthConstraint.priority = .defaultHigh   // from 1000 to 750
options: The priority changes and the layout updates
The app stops with an exception
questions.explanation: A required constraint cannot be lowered once it is active, and a non-required one cannot be raised to required either. The system raises an exception on the spot. If you expect to change a priority later, start it at 999 rather than at 1000.
whyWrong: That would be true for any other change — from 750 to 500, for instance. It is the boundary at 1000 that is forbidden.
Nothing is ignored: it is a loud failure, not a silent one.
Changing a priority never turns a constraint off. That is `isActive`.

questions.prompt: You set `isHidden = true` on a view inside a `UIStackView`. What happens?
options: It becomes invisible but keeps its space
It leaves the layout and the others close up over it
questions.explanation: This is the stack view's best feature. Everywhere else in UIKit a hidden view still takes up its space; inside a stack it is taken out of the arrangement and the rest close up, animatably. It removes a lot of constraint juggling.
whyWrong: That is what happens outside a stack view. Inside one, the space is reclaimed.
It stays in `arrangedSubviews`: setting `isHidden = false` brings it back with no further work.
Nothing becomes ambiguous: the stack recalculates with one view fewer.

questions.prompt: A custom view works out its own intrinsic size from its text. You change the text and the size does not update. What is missing?
questions.explanation: Auto Layout caches the intrinsic size: it has no way of knowing that something inside your view changed. That call throws the cached value away and asks for it again at the next layout.
whyWrong: `setNeedsDisplay` asks for a redraw, which is about pixels, not about size.
`sizeToFit` resizes a view to its content, but it does not tell Auto Layout that the intrinsic size is out of date.
Turning that back on would reintroduce the autoresizing constraints and make everything worse.

questions.prompt: What does Auto Layout do if two required constraints conflict while the app is running?
options: It breaks one of them and prints a long warning in the console
It ignores all of that view's constraints
It silently uses whichever was added last
questions.explanation: It would be no use to stop the app in front of the user, so it drops one constraint, shows something, and writes a detailed complaint in the console. That log names the constraints involved and says which one it broke — it is the thing to read, not to ignore.
whyWrong: It does not stop. It only does that for the priority change in an earlier question.
The other constraints are kept: only the one that could not be satisfied is dropped.
Which one it breaks is not simply "the last", and it is never silent: the log is always written.

questions.prompt: The parent is 320 points wide. How wide will `box` be?
options: Ambiguous: it depends on the order
questions.explanation: The second constraint is required and says "no more than 320 minus 40", which is 280. The first only wants 300, with priority 750, so it is the one that gives. The system then makes it as close to 300 as it is allowed, which is exactly 280.
whyWrong: 300 would break the required limit, and a required constraint is never given up for a preference.
320 is the parent's own width; the constraint explicitly asks for 40 less.
There is nothing ambiguous: priorities decide, not the order you wrote them in.

topics.title: Long lists: table and collection views
topics.summary: How a list with ten thousand rows uses the memory of twelve, why pictures end up in the wrong row, and the modern way to update a list without crashes.

lesson.heading: Who says what to show, and who reacts
lesson.body:
A `UITableView` knows nothing about your data. It only knows how to scroll and how to put rows on screen. Everything else it asks two other objects.

**The data source** answers two questions. How many rows are there? And: give me the cell for row number N. That is it — it is the whole contract.

**The delegate** is told what happens. A row was tapped. A row is about to appear. The user swiped to delete. You give it the decisions; the table does the mechanics.

This split is the **delegate pattern**, and it is everywhere in UIKit: one object does the generic work, another supplies the specifics. It is what lets Apple write one table that works for every app ever made.

`UICollectionView` is the same thing with a free layout: rows, grids, carousels, anything. Same data source, same delegate, plus an object that decides where each cell goes.

lesson.heading: Reuse: ten thousand rows, twelve cells
lesson.body:
A screen fits about twelve rows. If your list has ten thousand, building ten thousand cells would waste an enormous amount of memory for things nobody can see.

So the table keeps a small pile. When a cell scrolls off the top, it does not get thrown away: it goes back on the pile, and is handed straight back to you for the row arriving at the bottom. `dequeueReusableCell` is you asking for one from the pile.

The consequence is the thing to remember: **the cell you receive is not new. It is somebody else's old cell, with their data still in it.** So in `cellForRowAt` you must set **every** field. Setting only the ones that are not empty leaves the previous row's values showing.

`prepareForReuse()` is called just before a cell is handed back out. It is for clearing transient state and cancelling work in flight — an image download, an animation. It is not for configuring the new row: that belongs in `cellForRowAt`, which has the data.

And the classic bug, asked at interviews constantly. You start downloading an image for row 3; the user scrolls; that cell is now row 40; the download finishes and puts row 3's picture into row 40. The fix is to check, when the image arrives, that the cell is still showing the row you asked for — or to cancel the download in `prepareForReuse`.

lesson.heading: Updating the list without crashing
lesson.body:
The old way of changing a list is a minefield. `insertRows`, `deleteRows` and `reloadRows` animate nicely, but the table checks afterwards: "you said you added one row, so you should now have 11 — do you?" If the array does not match, the app stops with an exception, and the message about "the number of rows" is one of the most familiar in iOS.

So the order matters: **first change the data, then tell the table.** And every insert, delete and move has to add up exactly.

The modern answer is the **diffable data source**. Instead of describing the changes, you describe **how the list should look now** — that is a snapshot — and hand it over. The system compares it with what is on screen, works out the differences itself, and animates them. There is nothing left to get wrong, because you never counted anything.

Two requirements. The identifiers in a snapshot have to be **`Hashable`**, because that is how two lists are compared, and they have to be **unique** within the snapshot: two identical ones and it stops, because it cannot tell which row moved where.

One extra thing worth knowing: `reconfigureItems` updates a cell that is already on screen without taking a new one from the pile. `reloadItems` throws the cell away and builds it again. For a change to the content of a row that is already visible, `reconfigure` is both faster and smoother.

lesson.heading: Compositional layout: grids without the maths
lesson.body:
For years, anything more complicated than a plain grid meant subclassing `UICollectionViewFlowLayout` and working out every frame by hand.

**Compositional layout** replaced that with a description you build out of four nested pieces, and the order is worth memorising because it gets asked:

**Item** — one cell. Its size is given as a fraction of the group it is in, or as an exact number of points.
**Group** — a row or a column of items. The group is the repeating unit.
**Section** — the groups stacked up, plus headers, spacing and the scrolling behaviour.
**Layout** — the sections together.

So: **item inside group inside section inside layout.**

Sizes come in three flavours. `.fractionalWidth(0.5)` means half of whatever contains it. `.absolute(120)` means exactly 120 points. `.estimated(100)` means "around 100, work out the real value from the content" — that is how you get rows that grow with their text.

The thing that makes it genuinely powerful is `orthogonalScrollingBehavior`: one line turns a section into a horizontal carousel inside a vertical list. The home screen of nearly every media app is that one line.

lesson.heading: Keeping the scroll smooth
lesson.body:
A list stutters when `cellForRowAt` does too much. It runs for every row that appears, during the scroll, on the main thread. Whatever is in there has roughly a sixtieth of a second.

The four things that are usually to blame:

**Work that belongs elsewhere.** Decoding an image, formatting a date, doing a calculation. Do it once, somewhere else, and keep the result.

**A `DateFormatter` built each time.** Creating one is surprisingly expensive. Make it once and keep it.

**Cells that are not reused.** Check that the identifier is registered and that you are actually calling `dequeue`.

**Transparency and shadows.** A `cornerRadius` with `masksToBounds`, or a shadow without `shadowPath`, forces the system to composite each frame.

**Prefetching** helps too: `prefetchRowsAt` tells you which rows are coming soon, so you can start loading their data before they arrive. The important caveat is that it is a hint, not a promise — it can be skipped entirely during a fast scroll. `cellForRowAt` must still work correctly on its own.

questions.prompt: Why does a `UITableView` reuse its cells?
options: To keep each cell's state while scrolling
To keep memory and allocations down to the visible rows only
questions.explanation: A screen holds about a dozen rows. A list of ten thousand would otherwise mean ten thousand cells in memory for nothing. The table keeps a small pile and hands the same objects back out as you scroll.
whyWrong: Reuse does the opposite: it wipes out the old state, which is exactly why you have to set every field again.
They can be freed perfectly well. Reuse is a choice about speed and memory, not a limitation.
The animations come from the insert and delete methods, and work regardless of reuse.

questions.prompt: While scrolling fast, some cells briefly show another row's picture. Why?
options: The download finishes after the cell has already been reused
Images have to be set in `willDisplay`
questions.explanation: The closure holds that cell. By the time the picture arrives, that same cell has already been handed to a different row, and the old picture lands in it. The fix is to check, when the image arrives, that the cell is still showing the row you asked for — or to cancel the download in `prepareForReuse`.
whyWrong: There is nothing random about it: it hands back the cell that just scrolled out, which is precisely the problem.
The closure runs once per download. The trouble is that it runs too late.
`willDisplay` would have exactly the same problem: it is not about which method, it is about the delay.

questions.prompt: What happens if you run only this line, without changing the `items` array?
questions.code:
tableView.insertRows(at: [IndexPath(row: 0, section: 0)],
                     with: .automatic)
options: It stops with an exception about the number of rows
questions.explanation: After an insert the table asks the data source again and checks the arithmetic: there were 10, you said you added 1, so there must be 11. The array still says 10, the numbers do not add up, and it stops. The rule is: change the data first, then tell the table.
whyWrong: There is nothing to insert: the data source still reports the old count.
It is not ignored at all: it is one of the loudest failures in UIKit.
A full reload is `reloadData`, and that would hide the problem rather than cause it.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call `dequeueReusableCell(withIdentifier:for:)` with an identifier you never registered?
options: It returns the first registered cell
It raises an exception and the app stops
questions.explanation: The version with `for:` promises to always hand back a cell, so it has to know how to make one. With no registration it cannot, and failing loudly is better than silently showing the wrong thing. Register in `viewDidLoad`.
whyWrong: That is the older version without `for:`, which did return an optional. This one promises a cell.
It has no way of guessing which class you wanted. That is what registering is for.
It never substitutes another cell: that would produce a bug that is impossible to find.

questions.prompt: What must the item identifiers in a diffable snapshot satisfy?
options: Be `Hashable` and unique within the snapshot
questions.explanation: The system compares the old list with the new one to work out what changed, and comparing needs `Hashable`. Uniqueness is just as important: two identical identifiers and it cannot tell which row moved where, so it stops.
whyWrong: `Codable` is about saving and loading. It has nothing to do with comparing two lists.
They can be anything hashable: a `UUID`, a string, your own type. Numbers are not required.
Structs work perfectly well, and are the usual choice. What matters is `Hashable`, not being a class.

questions.prompt: What does `reconfigureItems` give you over `reloadItems`?
options: It updates the cell already on screen without taking a new one from the pile
It works with identifiers that are not `Hashable`
It does not need the snapshot to be applied
questions.explanation: `reload` throws the cell away and asks for a new one, which costs a dequeue and loses anything in progress. `reconfigure` keeps the same cell and just calls the configuration again, which is faster and visually smoother. Use it when only the content of a visible row changed.
whyWrong: Neither one recalculates the layout: they are about the content of cells.
`Hashable` is required either way: it is what the comparison is built on.
Both need the snapshot applied. That is how a diffable data source works.

questions.prompt: What is the right nesting order in a compositional layout?
questions.explanation: From smallest to largest: an item is one cell, a group is a row or column of items, a section is the groups stacked with their headers and spacing, and the layout holds the sections. Build it in that order and it reads like a sentence.
whyWrong: A section cannot come before an item: it contains the groups that contain the items.
A group holds items, so the item has to exist first.
A section does not go inside a group: it is the other way round.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `prefetchRowsAt` is correct?
options: It is called for every row before `cellForRowAt`
It always runs on a background thread
It is not guaranteed: `cellForRowAt` must still load the data itself
questions.explanation: It is a hint about rows that are probably coming, and the system is free to skip it — during a fast scroll it often does. So it is an optimisation on top, never the only place your data is loaded.
whyWrong: It is not called for every row, and sometimes not at all.
It replaces nothing: `cellForRowAt` still runs for every row that appears.
The callback itself is on the main thread. It is up to you to do the actual work elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What belongs in `prepareForReuse()`?
options: Configuring the cell with the new row's data
Clearing transient state and cancelling work in flight
Removing every subview and building them again
questions.explanation: It runs just before the cell is handed back out, and at that point it does not know which row it is going to. So it clears: wipe the old picture, cancel the download, stop the animation. Configuring belongs in `cellForRowAt`, which has the data.
whyWrong: At that moment there is no new data: the cell has not been assigned to a row yet.
Rebuilding the subviews defeats the whole point of reuse, which exists precisely to avoid that.
Reloading the table from inside a cell that is being reused is a loop waiting to happen.

questions.prompt: A self-sizing cell grows its text after a tap, but its height does not change. How do you force a recalculation without reloading it?
questions.explanation: An empty batch update makes the table recalculate every height and animate the change, without touching the cells. The cell keeps its state — a text field still being edited, for instance — which `reloadRows` would throw away.
whyWrong: `setNeedsDisplay` asks for a redraw. The height is a layout matter, not a drawing one.
`layoutIfNeeded` lays out what is there with the heights already decided. It does not ask for new ones.
`rowHeight` is not how self-sizing works, and 0 would just hide everything.

topics.title: Moving between screens
topics.summary: Pushing, presenting, and getting an answer back from the screen you opened — plus the architecture that stops a view controller from having to know what comes next.

lesson.heading: The navigation stack
lesson.body:
A **`UINavigationController`** holds a pile of screens. The one on top is the one you can see; a new screen goes **on top** of the pile and the old one waits underneath; going back takes the top one off.

That is why it is called a stack: last in, first out. And it is why the back button works without you writing anything — the previous screen is still there, with its scroll position and everything else exactly as the user left it.

`pushViewController` adds one, `popViewController` takes one off, `popToRootViewController` goes all the way back to the first.

The navigation bar at the top is shared by all of them, and each screen says what it wants in it through its own **`navigationItem`**: the title, the buttons on the right, what the back button should say.

And there is one detail that reliably trips people up. The back button shown on a screen belongs to the **previous** one, because it is the previous one's name. So to change what it says, you set `backButtonTitle` on the screen doing the pushing, not on the one being pushed.

lesson.heading: Presenting a screen over another
lesson.body:
The other way is **presenting**: the new screen comes up over the current one, outside the navigation stack. It is for something that interrupts — a form, a confirmation, a choice.

The style decides how it looks and behaves, and the default changed in iOS 13, which is worth knowing because old tutorials still say otherwise:

**`.pageSheet`** — the default now. A card that stops short of the top, the screen underneath still visible, and the user can **drag it down to dismiss it**.
**`.fullScreen`** — covers everything. The screen underneath is taken out of the hierarchy while it is up.
**`.overFullScreen`** — covers everything, but leaves the screen underneath in place, so transparency works. That is how you build a dimmed overlay.

Two consequences of the card being the default. First, the screen underneath gets no disappear callbacks, because it never disappeared. Second, the user can dismiss it by dragging, without pressing any button of yours — so if there is unsaved work, you have to stop them. `isModalInPresentation = true` turns the drag off, and the delegate tells you they tried, so you can ask "discard your changes?".

One more thing: a presented screen can call `dismiss` on itself. UIKit quietly passes the request up to whoever presented it. It is not wrong, it just reads oddly the first time.

lesson.heading: Getting an answer back
lesson.body:
Going forward is easy: you create the next screen and hand it what it needs through its `init` or its properties.

Coming back is the interesting half. The screen you opened has a result — the thing the user chose, the form they filled in — and the one underneath needs it. There are three ways, and each suits a different size of job.

**A closure.** One or two results, nothing complicated: `onSave = { ... }`. Shortest to write and reads well where you create the screen. Watch out for the retain cycle: the closure usually needs `[weak self]`.

**A delegate.** Several different events — saved, cancelled, deleted. A protocol with a method for each, and the property that holds it must be **`weak`**, otherwise the two screens hold each other and neither is ever freed. For `weak` to be allowed, the protocol has to be declared `: AnyObject`, and forgetting that produces one of the most common error messages in UIKit.

**A notification or a shared store.** When more than one screen has to hear about it, or the two do not know each other at all.

The mistake to avoid: having the second screen reach back and change the first one's properties directly. That ties them together so tightly that neither can be reused or tested on its own.

lesson.heading: Storyboards: segues, and passing data in
lesson.body:
In a storyboard the arrow between two screens is a **segue**. The system creates the destination and shows it, and you get one chance to prepare it: **`prepare(for:sender:)`**, which runs just before the move.

That is the only place to pass data in. Not `performSegue`, which only triggers it; not the destination's `viewDidLoad`, which is too late to be given anything.

The awkward part is that the system builds the destination itself, so you cannot use your own `init` — which is exactly what you need for dependency injection, handing a screen its view model instead of letting it build one. Historically you worked around it by setting properties afterwards, which means they are all optional and all mutable for no reason.

Since iOS 13 there is a proper answer: **`instantiateViewController(identifier:creator:)`**. You get given the `coder` and you call your own `init`, so the screen can have the things it needs as `let` constants from the first moment.

lesson.heading: Coordinators: taking navigation out of the screen
lesson.body:
In a small app, screen A creating screen B is fine. In a large one it becomes a problem: A has to know B exists, know how to build it, and know what B needs. Reusing A somewhere that leads to C instead means changing A.

The **coordinator** pattern moves all of that out. A coordinator is a plain object whose only job is to decide what comes next. The screen says "the user picked this" and nothing more; the coordinator decides what to show.

Two things it buys you. A screen becomes reusable, because it no longer knows what comes after it. And flows become testable, because deciding where to go is now ordinary logic rather than something tangled up with view controllers.

The trap everybody hits: the system back button. When the user presses it, the screen goes away but **your coordinator does not know**, so it stays in memory, and its parent keeps a reference to it forever. The answer is `UINavigationControllerDelegate` and its `didShow` method: it tells you which screen is now on top, so you can work out which screens went away and throw the matching coordinators out.

questions.prompt: On an iPhone with iOS 13 or later, what do you get from the default presentation style?
questions.explanation: The default changed in iOS 13: a card that stops short of the top, with the screen underneath still visible and draggable away. Before that it was full screen, which is why plenty of older tutorials disagree.
whyWrong: Full screen is what you got before iOS 13. You can still ask for it explicitly.
`.overFullScreen` is for transparent overlays and has to be asked for.
`.formSheet` is a centred box, and on an iPhone it behaves like a page sheet anyway.

questions.prompt: With storyboards, where do you hand data to the screen a segue is about to show?
questions.explanation: It is the one moment when the destination exists but has not appeared yet, and `segue.destination` hands it to you. That is the only place to pass data in.
whyWrong: `performSegue` only starts the move. The destination has not been created when you call it.
By `viewDidLoad` the destination is already building itself and nobody has given it anything.
`shouldPerformSegue` only answers yes or no. It does not get the destination.

questions.prompt: A pushes B. To make B's back button say "List", where do you set it?
questions.explanation: The back button is the name of the screen you would go back to, so it belongs to **that** screen. You set it on A, the one doing the pushing, and B shows it. It reads backwards, which is why it is asked about.
whyWrong: Setting it on B changes the back button of whatever B pushes next, not B's own.
A `leftBarButtonItem` replaces the back button with a custom one, and you lose the swipe-back gesture along with it.
`topItem` is whatever is on top right now, and it changes with every push. Not a reliable place to set anything.

questions.prompt: What is the real difference between `.overFullScreen` and `.fullScreen`?
options: `.overFullScreen` leaves the screen underneath in place
questions.explanation: With `.fullScreen` the screen underneath is taken out of the hierarchy, because it cannot be seen anyway — which saves work. With `.overFullScreen` it stays, so if your presented view is partly transparent, you can see through to it. That is how a dimmed overlay is built.
whyWrong: Neither can be swiped away: that belongs to the card styles.
It is the other way round: it is `.overFullScreen` that makes transparency useful.
They are genuinely different, and picking the wrong one gives you a black background instead of a dimmed one.

questions.prompt: Why does this not build?
options: The protocol is not limited to classes
`weak` cannot be used on an optional property
questions.explanation: `weak` works on a reference, and only classes have one. As written, a struct could adopt this protocol, and there would be nothing to make weak. Adding `: AnyObject` to the protocol fixes it, and `weak` on a delegate is what stops the two screens holding each other forever.
whyWrong: `weak` requires an optional. It is the other way round.
`unowned` would be worse here: the screen that opened this one can perfectly well go away first.
`@objc` belongs to the Objective-C world and has nothing to do with this.

questions.prompt: With coordinators, the user presses the system back button and the child coordinator stays in memory. How do you find out?
questions.explanation: The system back button does not tell your code anything: it pops the screen and that is that. `didShow` tells you which screen is now on top, so you can compare with what you expected, see which screens have gone, and release their coordinators.
whyWrong: A coordinator is not a view controller: it has no `viewWillDisappear`.
The navigation controller is still alive and well — it is the child screen that went.
Overriding a UIKit method in an extension does not reliably replace it, and it is not how the framework is meant to be used.

questions.prompt: B, presented by A, calls `dismiss(animated: true)` on itself. What happens?
options: A is dismissed along with B
UIKit passes the request up to A and B is dismissed
It crashes, being called on the wrong controller
questions.explanation: It works. UIKit notices that B is not presenting anything and quietly forwards the request to whoever presented it. It reads oddly the first time, but it means a screen can close itself without needing a reference to its presenter.
whyWrong: It is allowed, and it is the normal way of writing it.
Only B goes. A is the one doing the dismissing.
Nothing crashes: the forwarding is a deliberate feature.

questions.prompt: What happens if you run these two lines back to back?
questions.code:
present(alertA, animated: true)
present(alertB, animated: true)
options: Only A appears; B logs a warning in the console
Both appear, B on top of A
questions.explanation: A controller can present only one screen at a time. The second call arrives while the first is still animating, and UIKit refuses it with a warning: "attempt to present while already presenting". The second screen simply never appears — which is why the bug looks like "sometimes the alert does not show".
whyWrong: To stack them, B would have to be presented by A, once A is actually up.
Nothing is replaced: the first one stays and the second is dropped.
It does not crash, which is the real nuisance — the warning is easy to miss.

questions.prompt: How do you stop a card being dragged away when it holds an unsaved form?
questions.explanation: That one property turns the drag off, and the delegate's `presentationControllerDidAttemptToDismiss` tells you the user tried — which is exactly when you ask "discard your changes?".
whyWrong: `.formSheet` only changes the shape. It can still be dragged away.
That would stop the user typing in the form, which is rather the opposite of what you want.
Overriding `dismiss` does not catch the drag, and it breaks every other way of closing the screen.

questions.prompt: Which API lets you use your own `init` on a screen defined in a storyboard?
questions.explanation: The closure hands you the `coder` and lets you call your own `init(coder:)` with whatever else the screen needs. That is what makes dependency injection possible from a storyboard: the dependencies can be `let` constants from the very first moment.
whyWrong: That one creates the storyboard's starting screen and gives you no say in how.
In `prepare` the destination has already been built by the system: it is too late for an init of your own.
`UINib` loads a nib file; it does not give you control over how the controller is created.

topics.title: Taps, gestures and who receives them
topics.summary: How iOS decides which view a finger belongs to, what happens if nobody wants it, and why a tap sometimes does nothing at all.

lesson.heading: Finding the view under the finger
lesson.body:
When a finger touches the screen, iOS has to pick one view out of hundreds. It does this with **hit-testing**, and understanding it explains most of the "why does my button not work" problems.

It starts at the top of the tree and walks **down**. For each view it asks two questions:

**Can this view receive touches at all?** It is skipped entirely if `isUserInteractionEnabled` is false, if `isHidden` is true, or if `alpha` is 0.05 or less. Note what is **not** on that list: a clear background. A view with no colour at all still receives touches perfectly well — that is how an invisible tap area works.

**Is the point inside it?** That is `point(inside:with:)`, and by default it means inside `bounds`.

If both answers are yes, it asks the same of that view's subviews, **starting from the last one added** — the one on top, which is the one the user actually sees. The deepest view that says yes wins.

The consequence that catches everybody: if a button sticks out past its parent's bounds, it is visible — `clipsToBounds` only affects drawing — but it is **not** tappable in the part that sticks out, because the parent already said "not inside me" and the search stopped there.

lesson.heading: The responder chain: if nobody wants it
lesson.body:
Hit-testing finds a view. But what if that view does nothing with the touch? It does not vanish: it is passed **up** to the next object, and the next, until somebody handles it. That line of objects is the **responder chain**.

The order is: the view, then its superview, then its superview, up to the controller's root view, then the **view controller**, then any parent controllers, then the window, and finally the application.

It is worth knowing the one step that surprises people: after a controller's root view, the next responder is the **controller itself**, not the window. That is how a controller can receive something a view did not want.

The chain is also what makes two everyday tricks work. Sending an action to `nil` means "whoever in the chain knows how to do this" — which is how the system Copy and Paste menu works with no wiring. And `resignFirstResponder` sent to `nil` dismisses the keyboard wherever it is, without you needing a reference to the text field.

The **first responder** is the object currently receiving keyboard input, usually a text field. There is at most one at a time.

lesson.heading: Gesture recognizers
lesson.body:
Handling raw touches by hand — began, moved, ended — is tedious and easy to get wrong. A **gesture recognizer** does it for you: it watches the touches and tells you when it has recognised a pattern. Tap, double tap, long press, pan, pinch, rotation, swipe.

You create one, give it something to call, and attach it to a view. Two things to remember when nothing happens:

**`isUserInteractionEnabled` is false by default on `UIImageView` and `UILabel`.** Those two are meant to display, not to be touched, so you have to turn it on. This is the single most common reason a tap gesture never fires.

**A single tap fires on a double tap too.** The recogniser has no way of knowing a second tap is coming, so it fires as soon as the first one ends. To stop that, tell it to wait: `singleTap.require(toFail: doubleTap)`. Now the single tap only fires once the double tap has given up — at the cost of a small delay, which is exactly why iOS does not do it for you.

The other classic problem: you add a tap to the whole screen to dismiss the keyboard, and suddenly the table stops responding to selection. The recogniser has `cancelsTouchesInView` set to true, so it swallows the touch after recognising it. Setting it to false lets the touch through to the table as well.

lesson.heading: Controls: target-action
lesson.body:
A `UIButton`, a `UISwitch`, a `UISlider` are all **`UIControl`**, and they share one mechanism: **target-action**. You say "when this happens, call this method on this object".

The events worth knowing: `.touchUpInside` is the normal tap — finger down and up **inside** the control, so sliding off cancels it, which is what lets a user change their mind. `.valueChanged` is for switches and sliders. `.editingChanged` is for text fields, on every keystroke.

The older form passes a target and a `#selector`, which is an Objective-C method reference, which is why the method needs `@objc`. The newer form, `UIAction`, takes a closure instead: shorter, type-checked, no selectors.

And there is a memory difference worth knowing, because it is asked. **`addTarget` does not hold the target**, so if the object goes away, nothing leaks. **A `UIAction` closure does hold what it captures**, so writing `self` inside one creates the usual cycle — the button is owned by the screen, and the closure owns the screen. Use `[weak self]`.

lesson.heading: What to check when a tap does nothing
lesson.body:
Put together, the rules above cover nearly every case of "I tap and nothing happens". Going down the list in this order finds it in a minute:

**Is interaction switched on?** `isUserInteractionEnabled` on the view **and on every one of its parents**. One `false` anywhere up the chain and the whole branch is unreachable. Remember that image views and labels start with it off.

**Is it actually inside its parent?** If part of a view sticks out beyond its parent's bounds, that part is visible but not tappable.

**Is `alpha` above 0.05?** Fully transparent views are skipped. A clear background is fine.

**Is something invisible on top of it?** A clear view covering the area receives the touch first and absorbs it. The view debugger shows it in seconds.

**Is another recogniser eating it?** `cancelsTouchesInView`, or a gesture on a parent that recognises first.

**Is the button enabled?** `isEnabled = false` on a control means it ignores everything, quietly.

questions.prompt: You add a tap gesture to a `UIImageView` and it never fires. Most likely cause?
options: Image views do not support gestures
The target has to be nil
questions.explanation: `UIImageView` and `UILabel` start with interaction switched off, because they are meant to display rather than be touched. Hit-testing skips them entirely, so the gesture never gets a chance. One line fixes it.
whyWrong: They support gestures perfectly well, once interaction is on.
That property matters when a gesture is eating somebody else's touches. Here no touch arrives at all.
A nil target sends the action up the responder chain. It has nothing to do with the view being skipped.

questions.prompt: A button sticks out past its parent's bounds with `clipsToBounds = false`. The part outside is visible but does not respond. Why?
options: The parent fails `point(inside:with:)` and the search stops there
Buttons outside the bounds get disabled
The button must be brought to the front
questions.explanation: Hit-testing goes down the tree: it only looks at a view's children if the point is inside the view itself. The parent says "not inside me" and the search ends — it never gets as far as the button. `clipsToBounds` only decides what is drawn, not what is touchable.
whyWrong: Nothing disables the button: it is simply never reached by the search.
`masksToBounds` would also cut the button off visually, which makes it worse.
The order among siblings decides who is tested first, but here the search never gets inside the parent at all.

questions.prompt: Which of these views still receives touches?
questions.explanation: A clear background changes nothing: the view is still there and still receives touches, which is exactly how invisible tap areas are built. What gets you skipped is being hidden, having interaction off, or an `alpha` of 0.05 or less.
whyWrong: 0.005 is below the 0.05 threshold, so the view is treated as invisible and skipped.
Hidden views are skipped entirely during hit-testing.
With interaction off, the view and all its children are unreachable.

questions.prompt: Which event is the normal tap on a `UIButton`?
questions.explanation: The tap fires when the finger **lifts inside** the button. That means sliding off before lifting cancels it, which is deliberate: it lets the user change their mind. Using `.touchDown` instead removes that chance.
whyWrong: `.touchDown` fires the instant the finger lands, with no way back. Only right for things like a piano key.
`.valueChanged` is for controls with a value: switches, sliders, segmented controls.
`.primaryActionTriggered` exists and is useful on tvOS, but it is not the standard tap on iPhone.

questions.prompt: What happens when this button is tapped?
options: The action travels up the responder chain to whoever implements it
It crashes: the target cannot be nil
questions.explanation: A nil target means "I do not know who handles this — find them". The action goes up the chain and the first object that implements the method receives it. It is how the system Copy and Paste menu works without being wired to anything.
whyWrong: A nil target is allowed and is a deliberate feature, not a mistake.
Something does happen, as long as somebody in the chain implements the method.
The application is only the last link. Anyone before it can handle it first.

questions.prompt: Two subviews overlap exactly. You tap the shared area. Which one receives it?
questions.code:
container.addSubview(viewA)
container.addSubview(viewB)   // same frame as viewA
options: `viewB`, it is on top and is tested first
questions.explanation: Hit-testing goes through the children backwards, from the last added to the first — which is from the top down, the order the user sees. `viewB` is on top, says yes, and the search stops there.
whyWrong: Added first means at the bottom, and it is tested last. It would only win if B refused the touch.
One single view receives a touch. A second can only get involved through gesture recognisers set up to work together.
The container is only reached if neither child accepts it.

questions.prompt: A view has a single tap and a double tap. On a double tap, the single one fires too. How do you fix it?
questions.explanation: You make the single tap wait: it only fires once the double tap has given up. The direction matters — the one that should wait is the one you call `require` on. The cost is a small delay on every single tap, which is why iOS does not do it automatically.
whyWrong: That is backwards: it would make the double tap wait for the single, which always succeeds, so the double would never fire.
That changes whether the touch also reaches the view underneath. It does not change which gesture wins.
`numberOfTouchesRequired` is about how many fingers, not how many taps. That one is `numberOfTapsRequired`.

questions.prompt: You add a tap gesture to the view containing a table, to dismiss the keyboard. Now row selection stops working. Why?
options: Tables do not receive touches when there is a gesture
The gesture becomes the first responder
`cancelsTouchesInView` is true and cancels the table's touches
questions.explanation: Once a recogniser recognises its gesture, by default it cancels the touches that were already on their way to the views underneath. The table never finds out the tap finished. Setting `cancelsTouchesInView = false` lets both happen.
whyWrong: They receive them perfectly well. The problem is that they are cancelled halfway.
A gesture recogniser is not a responder and never becomes first responder.
`endEditing` only dismisses the keyboard. It does not touch selection.

questions.prompt: What is the next responder after a view controller's root view?
questions.explanation: The chain is deliberately built so that a controller sits just above its own root view. That is how a controller receives events that none of its views wanted — a shake to undo, a keyboard shortcut.
whyWrong: The window comes later, after the controller and any parent controllers.
The application is the last link of all.
A parent controller's view is further up, and only after the controller itself.

questions.prompt: Which statement about memory in target-action is correct?
options: `addTarget` does not hold the target; a `UIAction` closure does hold what it captures
questions.explanation: The old mechanism is deliberately weak, so a control holding a reference to its screen cannot create a cycle. `UIAction` is a closure, and closures hold what they capture — so `self` inside one, on a button owned by that same screen, is the classic cycle. Use `[weak self]`.
whyWrong: If it did, every button would keep its screen alive forever.
The closure does hold: that is exactly what makes the difference worth knowing.
It captures strongly like any other closure. Weakness is something you ask for.

topics.title: Threading and UI
